As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, the God-fearing will be in gardens and bliss﴾ up to the end of the verse... It is possible that this is an address to the people of the Fire, so that their being informed of it increases their grief and wretched state. It is also possible, and this is the more apparent, that it is an announcement to Muhammad (ﷺ) and his contemporaries: when He had finished mentioning the punishment of the disbelievers, He followed it with the bliss of the God-fearing, in order to show the difference and to encourage belief. "The God-fearing" here means those who guard against shirk, because they must end up in the Gardens. The more one's degree of taqwa increases, the more strongly the ruling of the verse applies to them; so that the God-fearing in general are, by the ruling of the verse, definitely (qat'an) assured by God, by the judgment of His true report. The majority of readers read "fākihīn" (fākihīn, enjoying), meaning joyful and delighted. Abu 'Ubayda said it is from the pattern of "laabin wa tamir" (laabin wa tamir, having milk and dates), meaning they have fruit. The qadi said the first meaning is more eloquent. Khalid, as transmitted by Abu Hatim, read "fakihīn", and al-fakih and al-fākih mean one who is pleased and lives in luxury. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿with what their Lord has given them﴾, meaning: from His bounty and His pleasure with them. As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of Hellfire﴾, this applies fully to those who guard against sins and will not enter the Fire; and it may apply to those who guard against shirk, on whom the threat is executed, in the sense: "and their Lord has protected them from the punishment of eternal abiding in Hellfire." It is also possible that "al-Jahim" (Hellfire) refers to one of the levels of Jahannam that is not a dwelling for sinful believers but is reserved for the disbelievers; so even if they are punished in a fire, they are not in the punishment of al-Jahim. The majority read "wa waqahum" with a light qaf; Abu Haywa read it with a doubled qaf for emphasis. All of this derives from al-wiqaya (protection), which is that which stands between a thing and what harms it. The meaning: it is said to them: ﴿Eat and drink with satisfaction﴾, and "hanī'an" (with satisfaction) is in the accusative as a verbal noun (maṣdar). As for His saying, exalted is He: ﴿for what you used to do﴾, its meaning is that the ranks of Paradise and its delights are according to deeds; but entry into it itself is by the mercy of God, exalted is He, and His covering with forgiveness. Eating, drinking and enjoying are not part of entering into anything; and the righteous deeds of servants do not oblige God, exalted is He, to bestow bliss as an obligation; but He, glorified is He, has made them a sign of whom His knowledge has preceded for bliss, and has tied reward and punishment to the acquisition (taka{s}sub) that lies in deeds.

As for His saying, exalted is He: "reclining" (muttaki'īn), it is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl), on the pattern of His saying, exalted is He: "fākihīn". The governing element for these two states is a verb implied in His saying, exalted is He: "in gardens"; other analyses are possible, but there is room for examination here. Abu al-Samal read "'alā sururin" with a fatha on the first ra'. "Zawwajnāhum" means: We made for each individual of them a spouse (zawj). "Al-ḥūr" is the plural of ḥawrā', who is the white one, strong in the whiteness of the white of the eye and the blackness of its black. "Al-'īn" is the plural of 'aynā', who is one with large, lustrous eyes together with their beauty. In the reading of Ibn Mas'ud and Ibrahim al-Nakha'i: "wa zawwajnāhum bi 'ays 'īn", Abu al-Fath said: al-'ayṣā' is the white one. 'Ikrima read: "wa zawwajnāhum ḥūran 'īnan". Abu 'Amr related from 'Ikrima that he read: "bi 'īsin 'aynin", with "'īs" in the genitive construction with "'ayn".

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 52, verses 21–28:

The words of the Mighty and Majestic:

﴿And those who believed and whose offspring followed them in faith — We shall join their offspring with them, and We shall not deprive them of anything of their deeds. Every person is a pledge for what he has earned.﴾ ﴿And We shall provide them with fruit and meat of whatever they desire.﴾ ﴿They will pass around among themselves a cup, wherein there is no idle talk nor sinfulness.﴾ ﴿And there will circulate among them young boys of their own, as if they were pearls well-guarded.﴾ ﴿And they will approach one another, questioning.﴾ ﴿They will say: "Indeed, we were before this, among our people, fearful.﴾ ﴿So Allah bestowed favour upon us and protected us from the punishment of the scorching wind.﴾ ﴿Indeed, we used to call upon Him before. Indeed, He is the Most Kind, the Most Merciful."﴾

The readers differed. Ibn Kathir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Ibn Mas'ud, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, Talhah, al-Hasan, Qatadah, and the people of Makkah read: "wa-attabaʿathum dhurriyyatuhum bi-imanin alhaqna bihim dhurriyyatahum" (with dhurriyyatahum, singular in form for the first and the second). Nafi', Abu Ja'far, Ibn Mas'ud (in one of the reported variants), Abu 'Amr (in one of the reported variants), Shayba, al-Jahdari and 'Isa read: "wa-attabaʿathum dhurriyyatuhum bi-imanin alhaqna bihim dhurriyyatihim" (with dhurriyyati-hum in the plural). Kharija reported from him the same as the reading of Hamzah. Ibn 'Amir, Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrimah, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak read: "wa-atbaʿnahum dhurriyyatahum bi-imanin ahlaqna bihim dhurriyyatahum." Abu 'Amr, al-A'raj, Abu Raja', al-Sha'bi, Ibn Jubayr and al-Dahhak read: "wa-atbaʿnahum dhurriyyatihim bi-imanin alhaqna bihim dhurriyyatihim."

Since "dhurriyyah" is itself a collective noun, the singular form is good in these readings; and since the meaning requires spread or multiplicity, the plural "dhurriyyatihim" is good in the reading of those who read it so.

The scholars differed about the meaning of the verse. Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and the majority said: Allah informs that the believers whose offspring follow them in faith, so that they are believers like their fathers, even if they do not match their fathers in piety and deeds, Allah will raise the children to the ranks of those fathers, out of honour for the fathers. A hadith from the Prophet (ﷺ) has come with this meaning, and they made the hadith the explanation of the verse. Likewise, there are reports indicating that Allah the Exalted shows mercy to the fathers out of consideration for their righteous children. Some people went away from taking this meaning from this verse, and that does not follow except by making the word "dhurriyyah" stand for their kind, as in the saying of the Exalted: ﴿Indeed, We carried their offspring in the laden ship﴾ [Ya-Sin: 41]. There is consideration in this. Ibn 'Abbas also said, and al-Dahhak: the meaning of this verse is that Allah the Exalted joins the young children to the rulings of the believing fathers in inheritance and burial in the graves of Islam, and in the rulings of the Hereafter in Paradise. Abu Hatim related from al-Hasan that he said: the verse concerns the adult offspring and there is nothing in it regarding the young children. Mundhir ibn Sa'id said: it concerns the young children, not the adults. al-Tabari related an opinion whose meaning is that the pronoun in His saying "bihim" refers to the offspring, and the pronoun after it in "dhurriyyatihim" refers to "alladhina", i.e., the adults followed them and We join the young children with the adults. This is a disliked opinion.

His saying "bi-imanin" is in the position of a circumstantial (ḥāl) clause. Whoever holds that the verse concerns the young children, then the circumstantial clause relates to the pronoun in His saying "attabaʿathum", so it is from the two objects. Whoever holds that the verse concerns the adult children, then it is possible that the circumstantial clause relates to the two objects, and it is possible that it relates to the following subjects. The most preferred of the opinions on this verse is the first opinion, because the verses all describe the favour of Allah the Exalted towards the people of Paradise, so He mentions among the sum of His favour that He cares for the good doer on account of the wrongdoer; and the word "alhaqna" requires that the one joined has some shortfall in deeds.

The majority of readers read "alatnahum" with an open lam, from "alata." Ibn Kathir, Abu Yahya and Shibl read "alitnahum" from "alita" with a kasra on the lam. al-A'raj read "wa-ma alatnahum" on the pattern of "af'alnahum." Ubayy ibn Ka'b and Ibn Mas'ud read "litnahum" from "lata," and this is the reading of Ibn Musarrif, and al-Qawwas related it from Ibn Kathir. The reading of the one who reads "alatnahum" with an open lam may be from "alata," for it is said: alata yulitu iltatan, lata yalitu laytan, ata yu'litu ilatan, alata ya'litu, alita ya'litu waltan; all of them have a meaning close to one another.

The meaning of this verse is that Allah the Exalted joins the one who falls short to the good doer, and does not diminish the good doer of any of his reward. This is the interpretation of Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Jubayr and the majority. His saying the Exalted: ﴿and We did not deprive them of anything of their deeds﴾ may mean: of their deeds, the good and the bad, and the pronoun in "amalihim" refers to the offspring. This is the interpretation of Ibn Zayd, and His saying the Exalted: ﴿every person is a pledge for what he has earned﴾ supports this possibility. "Al-rahin" means the one held in pledge, and in these words there is a warning. Abu Hatim related from al-A'mash that he read "wa-ma latnahum" without an alif and with an open lam; Abu Hatim said: this reading is not permissible in any way.

"Amdadtu al-shay'" means when you bring to it something else that increases it or that accrues to it. His saying the Exalted: ﴿of whatever they desire﴾ is an indication of what has been related, that when the bountiful one desires meat, that animal descends before him in the form in which he desired it. In Paradise there is no meat that has been slaughtered, and no effort is required in it of slaughter, skinning or cooking; in sum, there is no hardship in Paradise.

(p-94) "Yatanazaʿūn" means: they pass to one another. From it is the saying of al-Akhtal:

You contended with him for the purest wine, while the rooster had crowed and the time of the night traveller's nightly visit had come.

"Al-ka's" is the vessel in which there is drink, and "ka's" is not said of an empty one; so said al-Zajjaj. The majority of the seven and others read: "la laghwun" with a raf', "wa-la ta'thim" likewise; Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Hasan read: "la laghwa fiha wa-la ta'thima" with a nasb, by way of exoneration. On both readings, His saying the Exalted "fiha" is in the position of the predicate, and the predicate of the first has sufficed without mention of the predicate of the second. "Al-laghw" is falling-away of speech; "al-ta'thim" applies to the wine of this world both in the act of drinking it and in the actions that result from its drink; all of that is removed in the Hereafter.

"Al-lu'lu' al-maknun" is the most beautiful of pearls, because protection and concealment beautify it. Ibn Jubayr said: he meant that it is that which is in the shell, which no hands have touched. It was said to the Prophet (ﷺ): "If the young boys are like hidden pearls, then what of those they serve?" He, upon him be blessings and peace, said: "They are like the moon on the night of the full moon."

Then He, the Exalted, described them as being, in the midst of their bliss, questioning one another about their conditions and what each of them attained, and that they remember the state of the world and their fear of the punishment of the Hereafter in it. al-Tabari related from Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with them both, that he said: their questioning is when they are raised at the second blast. "Al-ishfaq" is the most intense fear and tenderness of heart. Abu Haywa read: "wa-wawwanā" with a shaddah on the qaf; the majority read it with its lightening, and 'Isa al-Thaqafi inclined "wa-qana" with the qaf lightened. "Al-samum" is the scorching; al-Rummani said: it is that which reaches the pores of a person, and it is the fire in this verse, and it may be said of the heat of the sun and of the wind: samum. al-Hasan said: al-Samum is one of the names of Jahannam. "Nad'uhu" may mean: we worship Him; this is strengthened by the reading of the one who reads "annahu" with an open alif, which is the reading of Nafi' (with a variant), al-Kisa'i, Abu Ja'far, al-Hasan and Abu Nawfal, meaning: because indeed He. The rest of the seven, al-A'raj and a group read "innahu" as a new, independent sentence. With this reading it is also good that "nad'uhu" means "na'buduhu" or means the supplication itself. For whoever takes "nad'uhu" to mean the supplication itself, it is possible to make His saying "annahu" with the fatha be the very supplication that was in the world. "Al-barr" is the one who is good and does kindness; from it is the saying of Dhu al-Rummah:

She came from the fair-skinned women, bare of clothing except for the thin cloth, and a kind mother and father.

Al-Tabari recited:

؎ ............... ∗∗∗ perhaps her husband will die or turn away from her.

It is said: "araba" and "raba" (both meaning to disturb). From it is the saying of the poet:

؎ .................. ∗∗∗ Indeed her unveiling this morning has troubled me.

And the saying of another:

؎ And indeed her speech has troubled me, O Hana...

Commentary of Ibn 'Atiyya (al-Muharrar al-Wajiz) on surah 52, verses 45–49:

His, the Mighty and Majestic, saying:

﴿So leave them until they meet their Day in which they will be struck senseless﴾ ﴿the Day when their plotting will avail them nothing, nor will they be helped﴾ ﴿And indeed, for those who have wronged there is a punishment short of that, but most of them do not know﴾ ﴿And be patient for the decision of your Lord, for indeed you are in Our eyes. And exalt your Lord with praise when you arise﴾ ﴿And during the night, exalt Him, and at the retreat of the stars﴾

His, the Exalted, saying: "So leave them" and what is similar to it of conciliation (muwada'a) is abrogated (mansukh) by the verse of the sword (ayat al-sayf). Abu Ja'far and Abu 'Amr, in one of the reports from him, read "yulqu" (يُلْقُوا), while the majority read "yulaqu" (يُلاقُوا). People differed regarding the day they were threatened with. Some of those who interpreted said: it is their death, one by one, and this is figurative. "Al-sa'q" (الصَعْق, being struck senseless): punishment in general, although its usage has become common for what befalls a person from an excessively loud cry and the like. It is possible that the day they were threatened with is the Day of Badr, because they were punished on it. The majority said: the threat refers to the Day of Resurrection, because in it there is a stroke that encompasses all creatures, but there is undoubtedly a difference between the stroke of the believer and the stroke of the disbeliever. The majority of reciters read "yaş'aqūn" (يَصْعَقُونَ) from "ṣa'iqa al-rajul" (صَعِقَ الرَجُلُ) with a kasra on the ʿayn. Abu 'Abd al-Rahman read "yaṣ'aqūn" (يَصْعَقُونَ) with a fatha on the yā' and a kasra on the ʿayn. ʿĀṣim, Ibn ʿĀmir, and the people of Makkah, according to the report of Shibl, read "yuṣ'aqūn" (يُصْعَقُونَ) with a ḍamma on the yā' and a fatha on the ʿayn, from "aṣ'aqa al-rajul ghayrahu" (أصْعَقَ الرَجُلُ غَيْرَهُ), meaning he made another person swoon. Al-Akhfash related "ṣu'iqa al-rajul" (صُعِقَ الرَجُلُ) with a ḍamma on the ṣād and a kasra on the ʿayn. Abu ʿAli said: it is permissible that it be from this, and it is like "yaṣrifūn" (يَصْرِفُونَ). Abu Hatim said: the people of Makkah opened the yā' according to the report of Isma'il.

"Yughni" (يُغْنِي) means: there would proceed from it any sufficiency (ghina') and defense (difa'). Then Allah, the Exalted, informed that for them, short of this Day, that is, before it, there is a punishment. People differed in specifying it. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, and others said: it is Badr, the Conquest and the like. Mujahid said: it is the hunger that struck Quraysh. Al-Bara' ibn 'Azib and also Ibn 'Abbas said: it is the punishment of the grave. Ibn 'Abbas, may Allah be pleased with him and his father, derived the existence of the punishment of the grave from this verse. Ibn Zayd said: it is the calamities of this world upon bodies, loved ones and wealth; they are a mercy for the believers and a punishment for the disbelievers. In the recitation of Ibn Mas'ud, may Allah be pleased with him, it reads: "short of that, near, but they do not know."

Then Allah, the Exalted, commanded His Prophet (ﷺ) to be patient with the decision of Allah, the Blessed and Exalted, and to persist in his warning and promise, by His saying, the Exalted: ﴿for indeed you are in Our eyes﴾. Its meaning: in Our perception and the eyes of Our protection and safeguarding, as you say: "So-and-so is watched over by the king with an eye." This verse is one that every believer should contemplate within himself, for it widens the narrows of this world. Abu al-Samal read "bi-a'yunā" (بِأعْيُنا) with a single, doubled nun.

People differed regarding His saying, the Exalted: ﴿And exalt your Lord with praise﴾. Abu al-Ahwas 'Awf ibn Malik said: it is the well-known tasbih, that one says at every standing: "Subhan Allah wa bihamdihi" (Glory be to Allah and praise be to Him). 'Ata' said: the meaning is: when you rise from every sitting. Ibn Zayd said: the tasbih here is the voluntary prayer (salat al-nawafil). Al-Dahhak and Ibn Zayd said: this is an indication of the obligatory prayers. So His saying, the Exalted, "when you arise" refers to the Zuhr and 'Asr, that is, when you rise from the midday rest (nawm al-qa'ila). His saying, the Exalted, "and during the night" refers to the Maghrib and 'Isha'. His saying, the Exalted, "and at the retreat of the stars" refers to the Subh (dawn prayer). Whoever said they are the voluntary prayers made "the retreat of the stars" the two rak'ahs of Fajr. On this view there is a large group, among them 'Umar ibn al-Khattab, 'Ali ibn Abi Talib, Abu Hurayrah, and al-Hasan, may Allah be pleased with them all, and it has been related as a marfu' report. Whoever took it to be the well-known tasbih made His saying, the Exalted, "when you arise" an example, that is: and when you sit, and in all your conduct. Mundhir related from al-Dahhak that the meaning is: when you stand in prayer after the opening takbir, say: "Subhanaka Allahumma wa bihamdika, tabaraka ismuka, wa ta'ala jadduka..." — the hadith.

Abu al-Ja'd Salim ibn and Ya'qub read "wa adbara al-nujum" (وَأدْبارَ النُجُومِ) with a fatha on the hamza, meaning: "and the ends (a'qab) of," and from it is the statement of the poet:

"So I became, from Layla at dawn, like one who looks / with the dawn at the tail of a setting star."

The majority of people read "wa idbara al-nujum" (وَإدْبارَ النُجُومِ) with a kasra on the hamza.

The tafsir of Surat [al-Tur] is complete, and praise belongs to Allah, Lord of the worlds.
